prompt.context: Your client is a craft beer company called Duck Island Beer Company out of Austin, TX. They are an international craft beer company beloved by craft drinkers around the world. They are looking to start selling beer in the United Kingdom. They want to know which style of beer to sell and if it would be profitable.
prompt.question: Which style of beer should Duck Island sell in the UK, and will entering the UK market be profitable?

clarifying_info.q: What is Duck Island's current market share?
clarifying_info.a: See Exhibit 1 — Duck Island holds 39% global market share, the largest single share among a small group of major players.

clarifying_info.q: What are Duck Island's current revenue and profit figures?
What beers does Duck Island currently offer?
clarifying_info.a: Over 50 brands split between lagers, ales, IPAs, and stouts.

clarifying_info.q: What is Duck Island's current strategy?
clarifying_info.a: Seeking rapid expansion and revenue in any way possible.

clarifying_info.q: Where does Duck Island currently operate?
clarifying_info.a: Everywhere in the world except the UK, Africa, and Australia.

clarifying_info.q: Is the UK a promising craft beer market?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the UK shows potential as a craft market.

exhibits.shows: A pie chart showing global beer market share among major players

exhibits.title: Beer Market in UK
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing total number of brands and number of competitors by beer style (Lager, Ale, India Pale Ale, Stout) in the UK market

framework: External / Market factors: UK craft beer demand trends, competitive landscape, barriers to entry, regulatory and tariff environment
Revenue: pricing strategy, volume projections, product-market fit by beer style
Costs: variable costs (brewing, ingredients, packaging), fixed costs (CapEx for local brewery), shipping and tariff costs
Market entry mode: brew in the US and export vs. brew locally in the UK
Strategic fit: alignment with Duck Island's rapid-expansion strategy and brand positioning

questions.prompt: Which beer style should Duck Island launch in the UK, and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibits 2 and 3 together. Exhibit 2 shows IPA has the least competition (fewest brands and competitors). Exhibit 3 shows IPA has the steepest upward sales trend (2013–2016). The combination of low competition and rising demand makes IPA the optimal choice. A strong candidate will connect US craft beer trends (IPA popularity surge) to the UK market and note this is a blue-ocean opportunity within craft.

questions.prompt: What qualitative factors would influence Duck Island's decision to enter the UK market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm in a MECE fashion covering: Internal — cash on hand for CapEx, knowledge of the UK market, marketing strategy; External — competition, barriers to entry, distribution channels, tariffs, regulatory concerns, converting a traditional beer culture to craft, shipping costs if brewed in US, local brewing costs if brewed in UK, US vs UK price points, supply chain expansion costs (hops, bottles, packaging); Other — legal drinking age in UK, Brexit implications, USD/EUR exchange rate volatility.

questions.prompt: Duck Island's strategy team has decided to enter with the 'Duck Island IPA.' Evaluate two entry methods — (1) brew in the US and export to the UK, or (2) brew locally in the UK and brand it as a US beer. Calculate profitability for each and recommend one.
questions.guidance: Candidate must structure the calculation: first convert barrels to bottles, then compute revenues, then compute costs for each scenario. Both scenarios yield equal first-year profit of $330,000, so the recommendation must hinge on qualitative factors and long-term outlook. Strong candidates note that UK brewing eliminates tariff exposure and shipping costs post-Year 1, yielding higher future profits once CapEx is recovered. US brewing preserves the 'imported American craft beer' brand premium but carries ongoing tariff and shipping costs.

math.setup: Given: 2,000 barrels sold in Year 1; price = $10 per 6-pack; 1 barrel = 165 bottles (12 oz) x 2 halves = 330 bottles per barrel; Imported: brewing $0.50/bottle, shipping $0.50/bottle, tariff $1.00/6-pack = $0.167/bottle; UK brewed: brewing $0.50/bottle, shipping $0.50/bottle (internal), no tariff, CapEx $110,000
steps: Total bottles = 2,000 barrels x 330 bottles/barrel = 660,000 bottles
math.answer: Both scenarios yield $330,000 profit in Year 1. After Year 1, UK brewing eliminates the $110,000 CapEx, giving it a structural cost advantage over the import option.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors would influence Duck Island's decision to go abroad (enter the UK)?

categories.name: Internal
ideas: Cash on hand for CapEx investment in local brewery
Knowledge of and experience in the UK beer market
UK-specific marketing strategy and brand positioning

categories.name: External — Market & Competition
ideas: Competitive intensity by beer style in the UK
Barriers to entry (distribution lock-in, shelf space, retailer relationships)
Cultural shift: converting a traditional UK beer culture toward craft

categories.name: External — Cost & Regulatory
ideas: Shipping costs if brewed in the US
Local brewing costs and availability of UK facilities
US vs. UK price points for craft beer
Supply chain expansion costs (hops, bottles, packaging, labeling)
Regulatory compliance (labeling laws, alcohol content rules)

categories.name: Other / Macro
ideas: Legal drinking age in the UK (18 vs. 21 in US)
Brexit impact on trade agreements and tariffs

recommendation: Duck Island should enter the UK market with an IPA, given rising IPA sales and the lowest competitive density of any beer style in the UK.

Both entry options yield identical first-year profit of $330,000; however, brewing locally in the UK is the preferred long-term route because it eliminates ongoing tariff and shipping exposure after the CapEx is recovered — though brewing in the US preserves a valuable 'authentic American import' brand narrative in the near term.
risks: Tariff escalation (especially post-Brexit) could make US-brewed exports uneconomical
Local UK brewery CapEx could overrun if construction or equipment costs rise
Consumer adoption risk: UK drinkers may be more traditional and slow to adopt American IPA styles
Exchange rate volatility could erode USD-denominated profits
Distribution agreements with UK retailers/pubs may be difficult to secure against entrenched incumbents
next_steps: Conduct detailed market research on UK craft beer consumer preferences and IPA acceptance
Evaluate and shortlist potential UK brewery partners or acquisition targets
Negotiate distribution agreements with major UK off-licences and pub chains
Develop UK-specific marketing campaign that leverages Duck Island's US craft heritage
Set a Year-2 profitability target accounting for CapEx payback and volume growth assumptions
